source_title: Natalie Portman Recalls ‘V for Vendetta’ Head-Shaving Scene (Exclusive) - People.com
source_excerpt:
The ‘Black Swan’ actress had to balance her nerves when doing the one-shot scene
Natalie Portman is revisiting V for Vendetta ahead of its 20th anniversary theatrical re-release
Portman talks to PEOPLE about how she felt before shaving her head for the film
Director James McTeigue also recalls the tense atmosphere while filming Portman’s one-take transformation
Natalie Portman remembers exactly how she felt before shaving her head in V for Vendetta.
The 45-year-old looks back on the film ahead of its 20th-anniversary theatrical re-release, specifically the scene where her character, Evey, and, by extension, Portman, had her head shaved.
“It was nerve-wracking that we only had one chance to do it,” Portman, 45, tells PEOPLE.
“I’m used to always having another chance in film, so it was scarier to have to nail the performance in one rather than be scared about the head shaving,” she explains.
James McTeigue tells PEOPLE that “the atmosphere behind the camera was hard sometimes,” especially when filming that scene. The director used three cameras to capture every angle, knowing they wouldn’t get a second chance.
“When you’re shaving off all Natalie’s hair, she’s like, ‘Oh my God, I’m gonna really do this,’ and she would be nervous,” McTeigue, 58, recalls.
However, McTeigue hired Portman’s actual hairdresser for the scene for a slight sense of comfort.
V for Vendetta follows Portman’s Evey, a woman living in a dystopian society who meets a freedom fighter plotting to overthrow their tyrannical government. The thriller, directed by McTeigue and written by The Wachowskis, is based on Alan Moore’s graphic novel of the same name.
Twenty years later, Portman notes that the movie still feels timely and relevant because “unfortunately, authoritarian governments are a continuing issue.”
“Even from the genesis of this project — the use of a Guy Fawkes mask — he fought against his own government planning the gunpowder plot in 1605, and then the graphic novel of V was written in the 1980s in reaction to the government at the time,” Portman shares. “So the project has always held a long timeline of the recurring theme of governments not serving their own citizens and citizens responding in protest.”
The Guy Fawkes masks have become the face of the movie and a broader movement, and Portman shares that she still sees them “every Halloween, but also often at various protests!”
In addition to Portman, the movie starred Stephen Fry, Stephen Rea, John Hurt, and Hugo Weaving as the mask-wielding protagonist.
McTeigue shares that Weaving, 66, “understood the physicality of the role and the right nuance for how V needed to be.”
“And Natalie is just a brilliant actor and person and is very well-read and erudite. I thought she really brought it, because V is on one particular journey, but, obviously, the audience point of view is the Evey character, Natalie’s character,” he explains. “The way she brings great empathy to the role was very important to me, and she did an amazing job at that.”
Despite making a very political and at times heavy movie, McTeigue says there were moments of levity on set.
“That’s the great thing about making movies,” he tells PEOPLE.
“You can have a very emotional scene with Stephen Fry, his character and how his character has never been allowed to be who he’s wanted to be for his whole life, but as soon as you call cut, Steven Fry walks off and makes a joke and is funny, and Natalie will do the same,” McTeigue recalls.
McTeigue says the actors’ performances have “almost nothing to do with me.”
“There’s a lot of great performances in that movie just because of the actors that are in it, and those actors that are in it are great actors. That’s what also makes the movie shine is their performances within the movie,” he shares. “They have a great script and I’m like, ‘Okay, that was amazing. Let’s try this or let’s try that.’ “
Overall, McTeigue “really loved making that movie, so there’s a lot that I put into the movie.”
“The script was a brilliant script adaptation. When audiences come to the movie, you can just watch it as pure entertainment,” McTeigue says. “You just take away what you wanna take away from it. It doesn’t matter what side of the political spectrum you’re on. It’s all-encompassing in that way. It’s just holding up a mirror to us in a lot of ways. But you can also go in and enjoy the action pieces and see stuff blow up, too, if you want.”
